newsitem.title: USA: Insurance merger wave seen continuing - analysts. [CORRECTED 20:16 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Insurance merger wave seen continuing - analysts. [CORRECTED 20:16 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects headline to show that it is analysts, not brokers, that see merger wave continuing).
By Matthew Lewis
The current wave of insurance broker consolidations is likely to continue but analysts are not certain that industry giant Aon Corp will be an immediate participant.
"There are a whole bunch of brokers left who could be acquired, especially in the U.K. and Europe," said Ira Zuckerman, vice president of Connecticut-based Nutmeg Securities.
Analysts said Chicago-based Aon, which earlier this month agreed to buy London broker Minet from St. Paul Cos Inc, appears to have its hands full at the moment.
Aon has been rumored to be interested in London broker Sedgwick Group plc, among others.
"They have to chew and swallow what they've bitten off, before they take another bite," said Jay Cohen, analyst at Merrill-Lynch.
The digestion process could take a year, although Aon in theory has the financial muscle to remain on the prowl for immediate acquisitions.
Aon spokespersons could not be reached for comment.
The company has also been busy consolidating Alexander & Alexander Services Inc and Bain Hogg, other recent acquisitions.
In addition to Sedgwick, London broker Willis Corroon Group is seen as another conspicuous acquisition target.
There has been speculation for some time that Sedgwick and Willis Corroon -- who rank among the world's biggest brokers, behind Marsh & McLennan Cos Inc and Aon -- will merge.
Sedgwick and Willis Corroon also have large U.S. and Asian operations.
"If Sedgwick and Willis Corroon merged, they would still be smaller than Aon," Cohen said. The world's big two brokers "have really distanced themselves from the pack," he said.
Marsh & McLennan in March agreed to acquire Johnson & Higgins, the third largest broker in the U.S., for $1.8 billion.
Another possibility is that if Marsh & McLennan were to buy Willis Corroon, it would virtually force Aon to buy Sedgwick, an analyst said.
"We used to talk about the big six global brokers. Now there's the big four," Cohen said.
The biggest independent broker in the U.S. is now Arthur J. Gallagher & Co.
"They're still independent, and I think they want to remain that way," Zuckerman said.
"(But) I think you'll see more consolidation, especially with the business getting to be more of a worldwide, rather than a country-specific, business."
The broking operation of Indianapolis-based Acordia Inc is for sale. Cohen said the company's brokerage business, excluding health care, is probably the sixth biggest in the world.

The industry's acquisition spree "is a reflection of what's going on in the commercial property-casualty business, where rates have been down under pressure for seven years, and show no sign of abating," Zuckerman said.

"Since for the most part, the revenues of brokers are tied to the premiums, its put a lot of pressure on their growth, and consequently made a lot of pressure to trim expenses to try to stay above water."
((--Hartford newsroom (860) 727-0224))
